stem: Which organisation keeps the World Heritage List?

options.rationale: Correct: the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization keeps the list.
SADC is a regional economic community, not the keeper of the list.
The AU does not keep the World Heritage List.
COMESA is a regional trade bloc.

explanation: UNESCO keeps the World Heritage List under the World Heritage Convention of 1972.

stem: Which of Zimbabwe's World Heritage Sites is shared with Zambia?

options.rationale: Correct: the Falls lie on the border with Zambia.
Mana Pools lies on the Zimbabwean side of the Zambezi only.
Khami is near Bulawayo, far from the border.
The Matobo Hills are south of Bulawayo.

explanation: Mosi-oa-Tunya / Victoria Falls (listed 1989) is a single site shared by Zimbabwe and Zambia.

stem: In which year was the Matobo Hills listed as a World Heritage Site?

options.rationale: 1986 is the year Great Zimbabwe and Khami were listed.
1989 is the year Victoria Falls was listed.
Correct: the Matobo Hills was listed in 2003.
1984 is the year Mana Pools was listed.

explanation: Mana Pools 1984; Great Zimbabwe and Khami 1986; Victoria Falls 1989; Matobo Hills 2003.

stem: Why was the Matobo Hills listed as a **cultural** rather than a natural site?

options.content: Because it has more wild animals than any other park in Zimbabwe
options.rationale: That would be a natural reason, and it is not true.

options.content: Because the Pioneer Column first entered the country through the hills
options.rationale: This is not why it was listed.

options.content: Because it contains the largest stone walls in southern Africa
options.rationale: That describes Great Zimbabwe.

options.content: Because of its rock art and the shrines communities still use
options.rationale: Correct: the long relationship between people and the hills was the reason.

explanation: Matobo was listed for its rich rock art and living religious traditions, showing a long relationship between people and the landscape.

stem: Mana Pools, Sapi and Chewore were listed mainly because of their …

options.rationale: That is Great Zimbabwe and Khami.
Correct: a natural site listed for its landscape and animals.
That is the Matobo Hills.
That is Victoria Falls.

explanation: Mana Pools is a natural site in the middle Zambezi valley, known for its pools and large numbers of wild animals.

stem: Finds of imported goods at Khami are evidence that its people …

options.content: were ruled directly by a government in Europe
options.rationale: Trade goods do not show foreign rule.

options.content: took part in trade with distant lands
options.rationale: Correct: imported goods show long-distance trade.
The finds say nothing of this, and the Torwa kept cattle.
Khami was built centuries before independence.

explanation: Imported goods found at Khami show that the Torwa state traded, through the coast, with distant lands.
hints: How do goods from far away reach an inland town?

stem: A newspaper reports that villagers near a World Heritage Site say they see little of the money tourists spend. Which change would **most directly** address their complaint?

options.content: Ban all foreign tourists from visiting the site in future
options.rationale: This removes the income altogether.

options.content: Remove the site from the World Heritage List
options.rationale: This would not give villagers more income.

options.content: Build a high fence to keep the villagers far away from the site and its visitors
options.rationale: This would worsen their complaint.

options.content: Share part of the fees with local projects and employ local people
options.rationale: Correct: this gives the community a direct share of the benefits.

explanation: Sharing revenue and creating local jobs gives neighbouring communities a stake in the site, which also encourages them to protect it.
hints: The complaint is about who benefits.

stem: Heavy rains cause part of an ancient stone wall at Great Zimbabwe to bulge and collapse. Which type of threat is this?

options.rationale: Poaching is illegal hunting of animals.
Vandalism is deliberate damage by people.
Pollution is contamination of air, water or soil, mainly by people.
Correct: natural forces such as rain loosen the stones.

explanation: Rain, roots and temperature changes slowly loosen stones: this is weathering, a natural threat.
hints: Was the damage done by people or by nature?

stem: Zimbabwe has five World Heritage Sites.
explanation: True: Mana Pools (with Sapi and Chewore), Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Victoria Falls and the Matobo Hills.

stem: Once a place becomes a World Heritage Site, it is owned by UNESCO instead of by the country.
explanation: False. The site remains part of the country, which promises to protect it; UNESCO keeps the list and gives advice.

stem: Match each World Heritage Site with the year it was listed.
explanation: Mana Pools 1984; Khami (and Great Zimbabwe) 1986; Victoria Falls 1989; Matobo Hills 2003.

payload.template: The name Mosi-oa-Tunya means "the smoke that {{blank:a}}". The World Heritage Convention was adopted in {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Mosi-oa-Tunya means "the smoke that thunders", after the spray and roar of the Falls. UNESCO adopted the convention in 1972.

stem: Identify **three** World Heritage Sites in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Any one of: Mana Pools (with Sapi and Chewore), Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Victoria Falls / Mosi-oa-Tunya, Matobo Hills
A second different site
A third different site

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Great Zimbabwe, Victoria Falls and the Matobo Hills.

stem: Explain **two** benefits Zimbabwe gains from having World Heritage Sites.

points.description: Identifies tourism / foreign currency
Develops: international recognition attracts visitors who pay fees and spend on hotels and guides, earning foreign currency and jobs
Identifies conservation support / pride / research
Develops: e.g. expert advice and training help protect the sites, or global recognition builds national pride

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: World Heritage status makes the sites known worldwide, so more international tourists visit; they pay fees and spend on hotels, guides and crafts, earning foreign currency and creating jobs. Listing also brings expert advice and training that help the country protect the sites for future generations.

explanation: One mark for each benefit and one for its development.
hints: Think of money and of protection.

stem: Poaching is reducing elephant numbers in a wildlife area in the Zambezi valley. Suggest **two** ways the authorities and communities could reduce it, and explain each.

points.description: Suggests more and better-equipped ranger patrols / anti-poaching units
Explains that poachers are more likely to be caught, which deters others
Suggests involving local communities (sharing income, jobs as scouts, rewards for information)
Explains that people who benefit from wildlife have a reason to protect it and report poachers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The parks authority could increase and equip ranger patrols, so that poachers are more likely to be caught and others are deterred. It could also involve nearby communities by sharing tourism income, employing local scouts and rewarding information, because people who benefit from wildlife have a reason to protect it and report poachers.

explanation: One mark for each measure and one for its explanation.
hints: One measure by the authorities, one that involves communities.

stem:
The table shows the results of a survey of 200 visitors to a World Heritage Site (invented for this question).

| Main reason for visiting | Number of visitors |
|---|---|
| Seeing the natural scenery | 90 |
| Learning about history and culture | 50 |
| Seeing wild animals | 40 |
| Other reasons | 20 |
| Total | 200 |

Study the table and answer the questions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What percentage of the visitors came mainly to learn about history and culture?

options.rationale: 50 is the number of visitors, not the percentage.
45% is the share for natural scenery (90 out of 200).
Correct: 50 out of 200 is 25%.
20% is the share for wild animals (40 out of 200).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Is this site more likely to be a natural or a cultural site? Give a reason from the table.

points.description: Natural site
Most visitors (90 + 40 = 130, or 65%) came for scenery and wildlife

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A natural site, because most visitors (130 of 200) came to see the scenery and wild animals.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest how the site's managers could use these results to protect the site.

points.description: Protect the features most visitors come for: e.g. limit building near the main viewpoints
Manage crowds at the busiest viewpoints with paths, timed entry or limits on numbers
Use fees to fund rangers and conservation, and provide education for visitors interested in history and culture

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Since most visitors come for the scenery, managers should stop building near the main viewpoints and keep the setting natural. They should manage crowds at those viewpoints with paths and limits on numbers. Fees should pay for rangers and conservation, and guides could serve the visitors interested in history and culture.

explanation: A data-response practice item on visitors to a World Heritage Site.

stem: This question is about Zimbabwe's World Heritage Sites.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe **two** threats faced by Zimbabwe's World Heritage Sites.

points.description: A threat described with an example, e.g. poaching of elephants and rhinos in the Zambezi valley
A second threat described, e.g. weathering and plant growth loosening walls at Great Zimbabwe and Khami, vandalism of rock art in the Matobo Hills, or building pressure at Victoria Falls

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Poaching is a threat to Mana Pools, where illegal hunters kill elephants and other animals for ivory and meat. At Great Zimbabwe and Khami, rain, roots and creepers loosen the stones, and parts of walls can collapse.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "World Heritage status brings more benefits than problems." How far do you agree?

points.description: Benefits: tourism, foreign currency and jobs; international recognition and pride
Benefits: conservation advice, training and support; research and education
Problems: crowding and building pressure; costs of meeting management standards; income not always reaching local communities
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
World Heritage status brings clear benefits. It makes sites such as Victoria Falls and Great Zimbabwe known worldwide, so more tourists come, bringing foreign currency and jobs for guides, hotel workers and craft sellers. It also brings expert advice and training in conservation, and it builds national pride because the world recognises Zimbabwe's history and nature.

There are also problems. More visitors can mean crowded paths and pressure to build hotels close to the sites, which can damage what made them special. Meeting the required standards of management costs money. Local communities sometimes complain that they see little of the income.

I largely agree. The problems are real, but they can be managed through good planning and sharing income with local people, while the benefits of income, protection and pride are large and lasting.

explanation: A practice evaluative item on the benefits and problems of World Heritage status.
hints: In (b), weigh tourism and protection against crowding, cost and fairness.
